items.cold_note: Trapped air 50 mL x 21% O2 = 10.5 mL O2; rise equals O2 used, so plateau at 10.4 mL = nearly all O2 consumed. Plateau is the same 10.4 for 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 g balls (and dry never plateaus at it), so A (wool exhausted) fails: wool mass varies 4x with the same ceiling. B fails: distilled still rising 5.8->10.3 after 8 hr. D fails: distilled water (no salt/vinegar) also reaches 10.3.
items.recognised_real_data: The classic steel-wool-in-an-inverted-tube demonstration that air is about 21% O2: water rises about one-fifth of the trapped volume and stops when the O2 is used up. A student who knows the demo picks C with no table; the stem's 'no tube rose more than X' points straight at the limiting O2.

free_elimination.how: 'stopped after 8 hr no matter how much O2 remained' is an arbitrary absolute time cutoff with no mechanism. It can be rejected from the stem and options alone.

items.note: Key recomputed: 0.21 x 50 = 10.5 mL; the ceiling of 10.4 is the same for 0.5/1.0/2.0 g balls and for the distilled tube, which has no salt or vinegar. no_source_needed yes: the textbook demo answers it, and A, the only rival, is refuted by common knowledge that 0.5 g of wool is not used up. Only one distractor is free, so R6 is not met.

items.cold_note: Both scientists accept that seedlings near adults survive poorly (3%) vs 30 m away (27%), whatever the cause (enemies vs resources). Monkeys/bats carry seeds up to 100 m away; without them more seeds land under crowns, fewer far away, so total survivors decrease. D reverses the direction; B/C ignore that dispersed seeds are the ones that survive.
items.note: Key recomputed from the intro data (3% near vs 27% at 30 m), which both scientists accept. no_source_needed yes: textbook ecology says seed dispersal raises seedling survival by moving seeds away from the parent (competition or Janzen-Connell enemies). With passage and viewpoints covered, a high-school biology student picks 'decrease, because fewer seeds would be carried away' and rejects D, its reversal. The Janzen-Connell vs resource-competition debate is real ecology, but no specific dataset is recognisable, so recognised_real_data is null. D duplicates the key's relation and reverses it (fewer carried away -> increase), which is a weak tell only.

items.cold_note: S1: full stomach adds weight and increases tug on the diaphragm (the cramping tissue). S2: swollen stomach presses and rubs against the parietal peritoneum (the irritated tissue). Both = more stress on the pain-producing tissue. A: neither says the stomach irritates the nerve directly. C: S2 says jolting not required; neither says harder jolt. D: S1 reduces flow to diaphragm, not abdominal lining; S2 has no blood flow.
items.note: Key confirmed. S1: a full stomach 'adds weight and increases the tug' on the diaphragm. S2: it 'presses against the lining and rubs'. A, C and D are each held by at most one scientist or by neither. Observation, not a defect: the key is the only abstract, mechanism-neutral option, a familiar 'both agree' shape. Without the viewpoints a solver cannot tell which of A, C and D belongs to whom, so I record no free elimination. The real-world cause of stitches is unsettled, and both views are real hypotheses (ischemia vs parietal peritoneum irritation). No fact error, because each is presented as a viewpoint.

items.cold_note: Exp 2 felt: 100 g 24, 200 g 24, 400 g 24 deg; critical angle independent of mass, so 300 g -> 24 deg. 17 is plastic, 36/12 have no basis.
items.note: Key confirmed: Exp 2 felt is 24 deg at 100, 200 and 400 g, so 300 g -> 24 deg. Consistent with real physics: the critical angle is arctan(mu_s), independent of mass. Background physics says the angle does not change with mass, but only the table gives the 24 deg baseline. With the source covered, 24 is not distinguishable from 17, 36 or 12, so no_source_needed is no. I checked Exp 3 for a fact error: a = 1.00 m x 2 / t^2 gives mu_k = 0.24/0.37/0.50/0.65 against mu_s = tan(17/24/31/38) = 0.31/0.45/0.60/0.78. mu_k < mu_s in every case, so the data are physically consistent.

items.recognised_real_data: Exp 3 is the textbook titration curve of 10.0 mL of 0.10 M HCl with 0.10 M NaOH, computed exactly: pH 1.00, 1.48, 2.28, 3.30, 10.70, 11.68, 12.30 at 0, 5, 9, 9.9, 10.1, 11, 15 mL. A student who knows the strong-acid/strong-base curve knows the jump sits at equivalence.
items.note: Key recomputed: changes are 7.4 (9.9-10.1), 0.6, 0.8 and 0.5. Correct chemistry, no fact error. no_source_needed yes: with the passage and table covered, knowing the titration curve shape (a steep jump at equivalence) plus the only option that is a narrow window bracketing a round volume selects A. The 0.2 mL window among three wide 4-5 mL windows is a strong option-set tell: an item writer would include such a narrow interval only for the jump. I did not list it as free_elimination because it picks the key rather than killing named distractors on an independent ground.

items.cold_note: 30 days / 6.0-day orbit = 5 cycles, peaks just after closest approach to the planet: exactly Scientist 2's stated prediction (geysers most active just after closest approach, 6.0-day cycle). A: star distance does not change on a 6-day cycle. C: S1 predicts drops in shadow, not peaks tied to planet approach. D: right scientist but a reason S2 never gives, and gas pulled away would lower pressure.
items.note: Key confirmed: 30 / 6.0 = 5 cycles, peaks after the planet closest approach, which is S2's stated prediction verbatim. D names S2 but a reason S2 never gives; gas pulled away would lower the pressure. A and C are refuted by S1's own predictions (star distance changes over decades; shadow causes a drop). The key echoes the stem's 'closest approach to the planet' wording, but D echoes it too, so the echo does not decide. Context (not an R5 finding): Nereth is a thinly disguised Triton. A ~5.9-day orbit, a ~165-yr parent orbit, N2 ice near -235 C, a thin N2 atmosphere, dark south-polar streaks from a single flyby, and the geyser-vs-wind debate are all real. Knowing Triton does not answer this item, because the question is which scientist a hypothetical observation supports. Real Triton's orbit is nearly circular, but the passage invents an elongated orbit for a fictional moon, so it is not a fact error.

items.cold_note: S1: glacier carried granite torn from the valley's head. S2: flood swept granite boulders down the valley from the mountain lake. Both: source is the mountains at the valley head. A is S2 only; C and D are S1 only.

free_elimination.how: The option set itself reveals the two rival mechanisms: A is a water/tumbling process, and C (with D) a glacier process. For a 'both agree' stem, an option committing to one rival mechanism cannot be the shared claim, which kills A and C with no passage. D (meltwater streams from a glacier) also commits to the glacier, so arguably it dies the same way. B is the only mechanism-neutral option.

items.note: Key confirmed: S1 says the glacier tore granite from the valley's head; S2 says the flood swept boulders down the valley from the mountain lake. Free elimination recorded: the option set spans the two rival mechanisms, so the neutral option is identifiable without the viewpoints (2 named, arguably 3). No second defensible option. Same 'neutral option wins a both-agree stem' shape as ASV5c-P7-Q2, but that is 2 items here, below the 3-item bar for a cross-item pattern; a full-batch grader should check whether it holds across all 'both agree' CV items.
